DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026 (The Copper Kettle)

**Verdict:** the price increases are reasonable, but the paper overstates what they will deliver. The risotto proposal rests on a misreading of the paper's own Table 1, and the case for removing it reverses once the table is read correctly.

## What holds

I checked these against the document:

- **Table 1 margins and volumes** are arithmetically correct. The plate counts sum to 1,050, matching §2.
- **The £810 a week (£42,120 a year)** is correct *as calculated*: 310 × £1 + 260 × £1 + 120 × £2.
- **"Below the competitor midpoint"** is correct for all three dishes:

| Dish | Competitor midpoint | Proposed price |
|---|---|---|
| Fish and chips | £17.98 | £17.50 |
| Burger | £16.50 | £16.00 |
| Steak | £29.50 | £28.00 |

- **The case for raising prices is sound.** Margin is slipping, prices haven't changed since September 2024, and the dishes are currently the cheapest in the local group.

## 1. The risotto has the *strongest* margin on the menu, not the weakest

Table 1 gives the risotto an **80%** margin, the highest of any dish. In cash per plate (£11.20) it also beats the burger (£10.80) and the curry (£10.90). Its sales of 90 plates are joint lowest, tied with specials.

The proposed replacement makes this worse. Specials run at **64%**. A vegetarian special at the same £14.00 and that margin would earn £8.96 a plate instead of £11.20. That is about **£200 a week less gross profit** (90 × £2.24), unless the new special is costed to match the risotto.

This is not a judgement call; the table settles it. Proposal 5.2 should be withdrawn. If the risotto is to be replaced for other reasons, such as freshening the menu, the replacement needs a target food cost of about £2.80.

## 2. The projection leaves out the beef increase in the paper's own §4

Beef rises 12% from 1 April, the same day the new prices start. Two of the three dishes being repriced are beef. If the whole plate cost of each rose by 12% (an upper bound, since chips, buns and sides aren't beef):

| Dish | Cost increase per plate | Weekly cost increase |
|---|---|---|
| Burger | +£0.50 | +£131 |
| Steak | +£1.25 | +£150 |

The offset is therefore up to about **£280 a week**. If beef makes up roughly 60–90% of those plate costs, it is around £200–£280.

**Corrected projection, if volumes hold:**

| | Weekly gross profit |
|---|---|
| Price increases | +£810 |
| Beef cost rise | −£200 to −£280 |
| Risotto swap, as proposed | −£200 |
| **Net** | **about +£330 to +£410** (£17k–£21k a year) |

That is roughly half the £42,000 in the paper. If the risotto proposal is dropped, the net is about £530–£610 a week (£28k–£32k a year).

Even after the £2 increase, the steak margin falls from 60% to about **58%**. The increase barely covers the beef rise.

## 3. The 71% margin claim doesn't survive these corrections

Using the five priced dishes (the specials' prices aren't given):

| Scenario | Main-course margin |
|---|---|
| Today | 69.9% |
| April, no action (beef rise only) | about 68.1% |
| Proposals as written, including beef | about 68.5% |
| Price increases only, risotto kept | about 69.7% |

The 71% figure exists only if beef costs stay flat. Measured against what April will look like without action, the price increases do help. But they hold the margin roughly steady rather than lifting it, and the risotto swap pulls it down.

## 4. "If volumes hold" carries more weight than the paper admits

The volume drop that would wipe out each dish's gain, allowing for beef:

| Dish | Volume drop that cancels the gain |
|---|---|
| Fish and chips | about 8% |
| Burger | about 4–5% |
| Steak | about 5% |

The case for volumes holding is weaker than it looks:

- **Loyalty cuts both ways.** Repeat guests are loyal, but they are also the ones who know the old prices.
- **The 2024 increase is not evidence here.** The claim that it "had no visible effect on bookings" is asserted without data. Bookings could also hold while guests switch from steak to curry within the same booking.

The direction of the volume effect is an open question. These thresholds are what the monitoring should be judged against.

## 5. Smaller points

- **Trading days.** §8 says "six trading days a week"; §2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is five. This doesn't change the weekly figures. Check the annual figure assumes 52 trading weeks.
- **Monitoring baseline.** Comparing April–May with January–February mixes the price effect with seasonal effects. Spring trade is usually stronger, which could hide a drop in volume. Use April–May 2025 as the comparison.
- **The monitoring plan triggers nothing.** It needs a threshold and an action. For example, if burger or steak volumes fall more than about 5% against last year, review those prices.
- **Lunch share.** "Weekday lunch... represents a small share of main-course sales" isn't supported by anything in the paper. Only the Friday–Saturday dinner figure is given. A till breakdown by service would settle it.
- **"Remain the value option"** (the author's wording) overstates the position. After the increases, the restaurant is no longer the cheapest in the group for any of the three dishes, though it stays below the midpoint for each.
- **Where the margin is slipping.** The 67% figure is across all courses, while mains are already around 70%. Some of the slide must be in starters or desserts, which this paper doesn't address.

## Suggested recommendation

- **Approve the three price increases.** Present them as protecting the margin against the April beef rise, worth roughly £28k–£32k a year in gross profit if volumes hold, not £42k.
- **Keep the mushroom risotto.**
- **Monitor against last spring's figures**, with stated thresholds for reviewing the burger and steak prices.
- **Separately:** consider a larger steak increase (it remains £1.50 below the midpoint), and investigate the margin on starters and desserts.
